paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A sample space is the set of every possible outcome of an experiment or random trial. It goes by other names too, such as possibility space or outcome space. It is usually written in set notation, with the possible outcomes, called sample points, listed as its elements. It is often labelled S, Ω, or U, where U stands for "universal set".

paragraphs.heading: What goes inside
paragraphs.text: The elements can be numbers, words, letters, or symbols, and there can be finitely many, countably infinitely many, or uncountably infinitely many of them. The outcomes must be mutually exclusive: if one happens, no other one does. A subset of the sample space is called an event, written E. If the experiment's outcome lies in E, then E has occurred.

paragraphs.heading: One part of a probability model
paragraphs.text: A well-defined, non-empty sample space is one of three parts of a probability model, also called a probability space. The second part is the event space, a well-defined set of possible events. The third is a probability measure, which gives each event a probability. You can draw a sample space as a rectangle with its outcomes as points inside, and events as ovals around the points that belong to them.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing the right one
paragraphs.text: A sample space needs the right level of detail for what the experimenter cares about, with irrelevant information stripped out. Often more than one sample space is reasonable. When you pull one card from an ordinary fifty-two card deck, you could list the ranks, Ace through King, or the four suits. Or you could combine rank and suit, giving a space with one outcome per card, fifty-two equally likely outcomes in all.

paragraphs.heading: Equally likely outcomes
paragraphs.text: When a sample space has N equally likely outcomes, each one gets probability 1/N. Throw two fair six-sided dice and record the ordered pair of numbers: there are 36 equally likely pairs. Four of those pairs add up to five, so the probability of a sum of five is 4/36. Not every experiment fits this mold, though. When a thumb tack is tossed, no physical symmetry suggests that landing point-up and point-down are equally likely.

paragraphs.heading: Infinite sample spaces
paragraphs.text: Some sample spaces are infinitely large. Measuring how long a light bulb lasts, for instance, gives the sample space [0, ∞). In an elementary approach any subset is called an event, but continuous sample spaces cause problems with that rule. So there, only measurable subsets, which together form a σ-algebra over the sample space, count as events.
